KEY MESSAGE 1...As of 2:45 AM EDT...Despite sfc high pressure 
building into southern Canada, a weak upper impulse is leading 
to fairly widespread high clouds across the region early this 
morning. These high clouds should gradually move off to the 
south /southeast over the next few hours, but have been thick 
enough to keep temperatures a few degrees warmer than previously
expected for most of the region. The exception is the ADKs, 
where there have been more breaks in the clouds and temperatures
are already in the upper 30s to low 40s per latest NYS mesonet 
obs. For the rest of the region, lows will be mainly in the 40s,
with some 50s possible near I-84. This means temps will drop 
several more degrees between now and sunrise as the high clouds 
clear out and winds gradually weaken. Today looks like a 
beautiful early fall day. With the sfc high sliding overhead, we
will see dry conditions with just some scattered high clouds 
around. Humidity will remain low with highs in the 60s.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Tonight into tomorrow, a sfc low will develop along 
a stalled frontal boundary over the Ohio Valley in response to 
another upper shortwave. This sfc low will track south of the region 
on Sunday, bringing widespread rain to the region. As the sfc low 
strengthens, so will the LLJ that will help advect more moisture 
into the region. PWATs rise to 1.5 - 1.75" per the latest HREF, 
which is high for mid to late September, albeit not 
exceptionally so. The sfc warm front remains south of our 
region, but with the sloping mid-level warm front lifting north 
into the Mid Hudson Valley, there will be plenty of warm 
advection/isentropic lift to provide forcing for ascent, as will
the right entrance region of an upper jet streak passing by to 
our north. Rainfall amounts have ticked up slightly for northern
areas, which are now expected to see a general half to three 
quarters of an inch. From around I-90 south, 0.75 to 1.5" of 
rain is expected, with some locally higher amounts possible 
closer to the I-84 corridor near the best mid-level forcing. 
With rain leading to wetbulb cooling Sunday, highs will struggle
to make it out of the 50s for most areas. 

Our thinking regarding hydro issues has not changed for Sunday:
aside from some nuisance ponding of water in the typical low-
lying, urban, and poor drainage areas, hydro issues are not
expected. We collaborated with WPC to have the marginal risk 
ERO trimmed back significantly with only the I-84 corridor now 
included. This now better aligns with our local messaging that 
given the lack of instability, stratiform nature of the rain, 
and high FFG values, flash flooding is not expected Sunday. In 
fact, this rain will be beneficial for most areas, especially 
the Mid Hudson Valley where <0.25" of rain has fallen in the 
last 5 days. 

Rain tapers to showers and comes to an end Sunday evening/night as a 
strong (1030 mb) sfc high builds E/SE into southern Canada beneath 
confluent upper flow. This sfc high will be the main driver for our 
weather through the first half of the week as it slowly drifts N/NE 
of our region, and will result in cool, dry E/NE flow. NBM has 
finally caught onto the drier solution we mentioned yesterday for 
Monday - Wednesday, as the strong sfc high should suppress any 
precip south of our region with low to mid-level dry air in 
place. The only exception is possibly Tuesday morning, when a 
few showers can't be ruled out near the immediate I-84 corridor 
with a passing upper disturbance. Given cool E/NE flow, highs 
each day will be mainly in the 50s (terrain) to 60s (valleys) 
with lows in the 30s (terrain) to 40s (valleys) each night.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Guidance has been hinting at a upper trough or 
closed upper low tracking from the Ohio Valley off the Mid-Atlantic 
coast late next week, and given that there has been some consistency 
in this signal for a few days we felt it deserves to be mentioned. 
As the ULL moves off the coast, a sfc low is expected to develop and 
strengthen as it tracks to the northeast. Some of yesterday's
12/18z guidance and tonight's 00z guidance indicates that the 
sfc low could come close enough to the coast to result in at 
least some rain for our area. Given that moisture looks quite 
abundant with this coastal low, we will continue to monitor 
closely over the coming days. That said, guidance is notorious 
for struggling with the placement of these closed upper lows in 
the medium to long range, so confidence in the track of the 
coastal low is quite low. Additional forecast changes should be 
expected over the coming days.
